cards.title: Max Levchin
cards.sub: 2001 · PayPal, Inc., Palo Alto — cofounder and chief technology officer
cards.prompt: Name PayPal's fraud-detection system and the man whose team ran it. Then say how many people that took, what fraction of the company that was, and who actually decided to freeze an account.
cards.body: Igor, run by Max Levchin. Technology Review found him heading "a team of 100 employees, about one-sixth of the company's personnel" who watched Igor's constantly changing graphics for red flags, alerts and statistical anomalies. Igor flagged; "humans review the evidence and decide whether to freeze the corresponding accounts."
cards.answer: Igor, under Max Levchin. About 100 people — roughly one-sixth of PayPal's staff — read Igor's graphics for anomalies, and a human, not the model, decided each freeze.

cards.title: The four-month fraud episode
cards.sub: July–October 2000 · disclosed in PayPal's IPO prospectus
cards.prompt: PayPal's prospectus dates one fraud episode to the month. Give its four months and its cost in gross unauthorised charge-backs — then set that against what PayPal earned and provisioned over the first nine months of the same year.
cards.body: "During the four months between July and October 2000, we experienced a significant fraud episode and, as a result, we incurred gross losses due to unauthorized charge-backs totaling $5.7 million" — 64.0% of that year's unauthorised charge-backs. Nine-month revenue: $5.6 million. Provision for transaction losses: $7.7 million.
cards.answer: July to October 2000, $5.7 million of gross unauthorised charge-backs — 64% of the year's total. Against $5.6 million of revenue and a $7.7 million loss provision for the nine months to 30 September 2000: the fraud outran the business.

cards.title: Adversarial Classification
cards.sub: KDD'04, Seattle, 22–25 August 2004 · University of Washington
cards.prompt: PayPal could not automate its fraud desk away, and a 2004 KDD paper says why. Give both halves of its claim: what happens to a classifier once it is deployed against an adversary, and the only remedy the authors say was available at the time.
cards.body: Dalvi, Domingos, Mausam, Sanghai and Verma, "Adversarial Classification", KDD'04, Seattle. Classification is modelled as a game between classifier and adversary, each move making the other's model stale. Their own bound: "While complete automation will never be possible…" Until then: "repeated, manual, ad hoc reconstruction of the classifier."
cards.answer: "Adversarial Classification" (Dalvi, Domingos, Mausam, Sanghai, Verma) at KDD'04. The only remedy then on offer was repeated, manual, ad hoc reconstruction of the classifier — a person rebuilding it by hand, forever.

cards.title: Shipping the engineer with the software
cards.sub: 2003 → Palantir's 2020 S-1 → the decomp round you will sit
cards.prompt: PayPal never got the human out of the loop. Name the PayPal cofounder who built a company on that fact, the company, the job title it invented for the person posted beside the analyst, and the price its 2020 filing puts on the arrangement.
cards.body: Palantir, 2003. Its S-1 says the hard problems "can only be solved by working directly with customers" and that "custom code and consulting teams are unsustainable alternatives" — so it ships forward deployed engineers instead, and keeps them on a customer "even if those allocations reduce contribution margin". Losses every year since inception.
cards.answer: Peter Thiel; Palantir Technologies, 2003; the forward deployed engineer (FDE). The S-1 keeps FDEs allocated to a customer even when it reduces contribution margin, and reports a loss every year since inception — $579.6 million in 2019.
